title: Union types (A | B) and exhaustiveness
hook: A union type says a value can be one of several shapes — like a function parameter that accepts either a string or a number. TypeScript checks that you handle every possibility before you use the value safely.

blocks.text: A **union type** is written `A | B` and means "this value is either type A or type B." Unlike C#, which has no first-class union syntax, TypeScript unions are **structural** — the compiler tracks which members are safe on every branch. The special type **`never`** represents values that should not exist; returning `never` from a function that takes a union proves you handled every case (**exhaustiveness**). Unions are erased at run time — JavaScript still sees a plain value; TypeScript only enforces the contract at compile time.

entries.plainDefinition: A type that allows a value to be one of several alternatives. You must narrow before using members that are not shared by every alternative.
entries.example: `string | number` — a parameter can be text or a numeric score.

entries.plainDefinition: The compiler verifies that every member of a union was handled, often by assigning the remaining type to `never` in a default branch.
entries.example: `default: const _exhaustive: never = value;` — compile error if a case is missing.

entries.plainDefinition: The empty set of values. Used for impossible branches, functions that never return, and proving exhaustive switches.
entries.example: `function fail(msg: string): never { throw new Error(msg); }`

blocks.text: API responses, form fields, and event payloads rarely have a single shape. A payment status might be `"pending" | "paid" | "failed"`. Without unions you fall back to `string` or `any` and lose compile-time safety. Unions let you model optional states (`T | null`), multiple input kinds (`string | File`), and polymorphic results — the same pattern C# approximates with inheritance, interfaces, or `OneOf` libraries, but with lighter syntax.

blocks.title: Compile-time only
blocks.body: Unions exist only in the type checker. At run time JavaScript sees `typeof x === "string"` checks — TypeScript does not emit union metadata. Every union branch still needs a narrowing guard before you access type-specific members.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Declare the union
items.body: `type Id = string | number;` — callers may pass either form.

items.title: Find shared members
items.body: Only properties and methods present on **every** branch are usable without narrowing. `string | number` shares no useful methods beyond coercion.

items.title: Narrow with a guard
items.body: `if (typeof id === "string")` — inside the block, `id` is `string`. See the widening/narrowing topic for the full toolkit.

items.title: Prove exhaustiveness
items.body: In `switch`, use `default` with `const _check: never = value` so adding a new union member forces a compile error.

diagram.title: Union narrowing flow
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  U["value: string | number"] --> G{"typeof check"}
  G -->|string| S["branch: string"]
  G -->|number| N["branch: number"]
  G -->|neither| E["never — should not happen"]
  S --> OK["Safe to call .toUpperCase()"]
  N --> OK2["Safe to call .toFixed()"]

snippet.label: Basic union parameter
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `UserId` is a type alias for a union. Line 4: `typeof` narrows to `string` — `.trim()` is legal. Line 7: the `else` branch is inferred as `number`. Line 10–11: both call sites type-check because each literal fits the union.

snippet.label: Exhaustive switch with never
snippet.explanation: Line 1: string literal union — each string is a distinct type member. Lines 4–7: each case narrows `status`. Lines 8–11: if you add `"refunded"` to the union but forget a `case`, `status` is no longer `never` and the assignment fails at compile time.

snippet.label: Union with null — optional API field
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `string | null` models a field that may be missing at the object level (not the same as optional `?`). Line 4: comparing to `null` narrows away null. Line 7: TypeScript knows `avatarUrl` is `string` — no optional chaining needed.

snippet.label: Failure mode — using without narrowing
snippet.explanation: Line 3: neither `toFixed` (number) nor string methods are safe on the union. Line 6: you cannot assign a union to a single branch type without narrowing. This is the core safety unions provide — the error appears at compile time, not in production.

blocks.title: Unions across languages
rows: No `|` — use base type + `is` / pattern matching
`T?` for value types; NRT for references

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Accessing branch-specific members without narrowing — always guard first. Widening a literal union to `string` accidentally by reassigning to a `let` variable (see widening topic). Using `as string` to silence the compiler instead of a real guard — hides bugs that unions are meant to catch.

blocks.text: Unions are the backbone of API boundary modeling: `unknown` at the edge, narrow to a discriminated union internally. **Distributive behavior** appears when unions interact with conditional types (module 12) — `T extends U ? X : Y` distributes over `T` when `T` is a naked type parameter. Union assignability is symmetric for literals: `"a"` is assignable to `string | number` but not vice versa. Prefer literal unions over `string` enums for tree-shakeable, JSON-friendly tags. In production, log the `never` branch in default cases during development, then strip for release builds if needed.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying unions exist at run time. Claiming `string | number` lets you call any method on the value. Not knowing how `never` proves exhaustiveness. Confusing union (`|`) with intersection (`&`).

interviewTakeaways: Union `A | B` means the value is one alternative — narrow before branch-specific access.
Unions are erased at compile time; JavaScript only sees the runtime value.
`never` in a default branch proves exhaustive handling of a finite union.
Literal unions (`"a" | "b"`) are preferable to `string` when the set is fixed.
60s: Union is OR at the type level. Narrow with typeof, in, or discriminant. never catches missing cases. C# uses patterns instead of | syntax.
commonPitfalls: Using branch-specific members without narrowing — TS2339 at compile time.
Widening `"pending"` to `string` and losing literal exhaustiveness.
Strong answer: 'Union is compile-time OR. Narrow first. never for exhaustiveness. Erased at runtime like all TS types.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript `typeof` and `instanceof` are the runtime counterparts to TypeScript narrowing. Unions add compile-time proof that checks exist.
C# models alternatives with inheritance, interfaces, or records plus `switch` patterns. TypeScript unions are structural and lighter but require explicit narrowing.
